forces.title: High costs hinder adoption of low-carbon shipping fuels like biomethanol
forces.description: The high cost of low-carbon shipping fuels, including bio-methanol, relative to their benefits is cited by 40% of surveyed cargo owners as the primary barrier to adoption. This makes achieving cost parity with conventional fuels uncertain, slowing the decarbonization trajectory and impacting the supply-side demand for these alternative fuels in Europe.
forces.source_title: Demand for Low-Carbon Shipping Has Fallen, but Long-Term Value Persists

forces.title: European cargo owners show reduced willingness-to-pay for low-carbon shipping
forces.description: The share of European cargo owners willing to pay a premium for low-carbon shipping (which relies on alternative fuels like biomethanol) has declined from 5% to 3.5%. This indicates a structural shift where the previous upward trend in willingness-to-pay has ended, driven by regulatory uncertainty, tighter budgets, and weaker near-term economics for shipping companies.
forces.source_title: Demand for Low-Carbon Shipping Has Fallen, but Long-Term Value Persists

forces.title: Policy, technology, and biomass competition limit full biogas potential
forces.description: While biogas has the theoretical capacity to supply one-third of Europe's current gas demand, realizing this potential is challenging. It depends on robust policy support, rapid technological deployment of advanced gasification, and effective management of competition for sustainable biomass feedstocks (manure, agricultural residues, organic waste), conditions currently not fully met.
forces.source_title: How Europe can reduce reliance on imported gas and what it means for business…

forces.title: Renewed energy crises boost investment case for local biogas production
forces.description: Prior to recent energy crises, biogas was considered expensive compared to conventional gas. However, a renewed energy crisis could significantly strengthen the economic case for investing in higher-priced, locally produced biogas. This enhances energy independence and reduces exposure to volatile international energy markets, making it a strategic investment for Europe.
forces.source_title: How Europe can reduce reliance on imported gas and what it means for business…

forces.title: Biogas provides strategic energy independence and market volatility resilience
forces.description: Investing in locally produced biogas, despite higher costs, offers a strategic move for businesses to reduce exposure to volatile international energy markets and strengthen energy independence. This resilience is increasingly crucial for competitiveness, shifting focus from solely optimizing short-term fuel costs to integrating energy security into investment decisions across Europe.
forces.source_title: How Europe can reduce reliance on imported gas and what it means for business…

forces.title: FuelEU Maritime Regulation mandates gradual reduction in ship fuel emissions
forces.description: The FuelEU Maritime Regulation, effective January 2025, requires a gradual reduction in the greenhouse gas intensity of ship fuel in Europe. Its primary aim is to increase the use of alternative fuels, including biofuels, which will drive demand for their production and supply to the maritime sector, supporting market growth for Bioenergy & Alternative Fuels.

forces.title: Significant barriers impede alternative biofuel adoption in Norwegian shipping
forces.description: The Norwegian maritime industry faces substantial barriers to wider adoption of alternative fuels, including biofuels, for decarbonization. These include a critical lack of onshore infrastructure, high prices for alternative fuels, significant investment costs for shipowners, limited availability of these fuels, and lingering technological uncertainties surrounding their deployment and use.

forces.title: Industry advocates for government plan supporting alternative fuel production
forces.description: The Norwegian Shipowners' Association encourages Norwegian authorities to present a plan for the production and use of alternative fuels, including biofuels, and implement guarantee schemes like contracts for difference. Such policy instruments are crucial to scale up and roll out climate and environmental technology, supporting the supply side of alternative fuels.

forces.title: Massive grid investments planned to integrate growing biomass-based energy
forces.description: European grid operators are set for significant investments, with yearly capital expenditure projected to reach €95bn by 2030 and €157bn by 2040. These investments are deemed necessary to accommodate the increasing volumes of green energy coming online, explicitly including biomass. This infrastructure upgrade will facilitate the integration and distribution of bioenergy across Europe.
forces.source_title: European Utilities: Big investments and bigger debt

viewpoints.title: Low-carbon shipping fuel demand faces decline, impacting bioenergy prospects
viewpoints.description: European cargo owners' willingness-to-pay for low-carbon shipping (including fuels like biomethanol) has declined from 5% to 3.5%, indicating an end to the previous upward trajectory. High costs relative to benefits (40% citing it as primary barrier) and regulatory uncertainty drive this price sensitivity, impacting the demand outlook for alternative fuels like biomethanol.
viewpoints.source_title: Demand for Low-Carbon Shipping Has Fallen, but Long-Term Value Persists

viewpoints.title: Biogas seen as a key scalable, local, and circular solution for Europe
viewpoints.description: Biogas production offers meaningful potential for Europe to reduce reliance on imported gas, acting as a local, circular energy solution. Forecasts suggest production could triple by 2030 to over 20 bcm and reach 30 bcm by 2035. While falling short of the REPowerEU target, biogas has theoretical capacity for one-third of current gas demand, strengthening energy independence.
viewpoints.source_title: How Europe can reduce reliance on imported gas and what it means for business…

viewpoints.title: Biofuel considered most viable transition fuel for Norwegian maritime sector
viewpoints.description: The Norwegian Shipowners' Association's members rank biofuel as the most viable fuel option for transitioning the fleet towards low and zero emissions, particularly for the period leading up to 2050. This indicates a strategic shift towards more readily available transition fuels, acknowledging that the full shift to zero-emission fuels might occur later than initially anticipated.

demand_drivers.description: Biogas production reduces reliance on volatile international gas markets and strengthens energy independence for Europe.
Biogas production utilizes sustainable feedstocks such as manure, agricultural residues, and organic waste, promoting a circular economy approach.
Scaling up biogas production requires robust policy support and reliable buyers willing to pay a green premium for biogas.

pnl_drivers.description: Biogas production costs currently range from €50 to €100 per MWh, which was historically expensive compared to gas prices around €20 per MWh prior to recent energy crises.

new_opportunities.description: Tapping into all available sustainable feedstocks, including advanced gasification technologies, could allow biogas to supply up to one-third of Europe's current gas demand.

market_sizing.methodology: Europe's current annual biogas production, representing 1.6% of current gas demand. Forecasts from DNV and BNEF project production to increase to over 20 BCM by 2030 and 30 BCM by 2035 (equating to ~8% of current gas demand), though this falls short of the EU’s 35 BCM REPowerEU target for 2030. Theoretical capacity could reach one-third of current gas demand.
market_sizing.source_title: How Europe can reduce reliance on imported gas and what it means for business…
